summary: Describes techniques that let LISP sites communicate with Internet sites not running LISP, using IPv4, IPv6 or both. LISP sites use endpoint identifiers instead of ordinary addresses, so special helper devices are needed. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A person who uses a new style of address needs a translator to chat with people who still use the old style. This describes those translators.

questions: how do lisp sites talk to non-lisp sites
subtitle: How sites that use LISP identifiers and sites that do not can still exchange traffic.

tldr.problem: LISP sites use endpoint identifiers (EIDs) that are normally not routed in the global Internet, so ordinary non-LISP sites cannot reach them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes three helpers: Proxy-ITRs that attract traffic for EID space and encapsulate it, LISP-NAT that swaps non-routable EIDs for routable addresses, and Proxy-ETRs that carry LISP-site traffic out to non-LISP sites.
tldr.outcome: These mechanisms are Experimental, and the RFC warns they may be hard to deploy or may have unintended effects on applications until open questions are understood.

today: RFC 6832 is an Experimental specification from January 2013, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 6830, and the RFC itself says several areas remained open for further study.

sections.title: The Interworking Problem
sections.content:
In LISP, EID-Prefixes are normally not advertised into the Internet's Default-Free Zone (DFZ); only Routing Locators (RLOCs) are carried there. Yet existing non-LISP sites must still be able to reach sites numbered from EID space. This document describes three mechanisms for that.

The Proxy-ITR acts as an intermediate Ingress Tunnel Router for non-LISP hosts. LISP-NAT adds a form of Network Address Translation to tunnel routers so routable addresses replace non-routable EIDs. The Proxy-ETR acts as an intermediate Egress Tunnel Router for LISP sites whose packets to non-LISP sites need encapsulation. Any interworking model should be independent of the particular EID-to-RLOC mapping algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Some houses have addresses that the regular mail trucks do not know. These helpers pick up the mail and carry it the rest of the way.

sections.title: The Four Connectivity Cases
sections.content:
There are four unicast cases: non-LISP to non-LISP, LISP to LISP, LISP to non-LISP, and non-LISP to LISP. The first is today's Internet and the second is covered by RFC 6830.

In the third case, a LISP site can usually send directly because non-LISP prefixes are routable. The ITR knows the destination is non-LISP when it matches a negative Map-Cache entry with the action Natively-Forward.

The fourth case is the hardest. If a non-LISP host sends to a non-routable EID, the packet is forwarded inside the source site until a router with no default route drops it. Something must make the destination EID routable; Proxy-ITRs and LISP-NAT are two such mechanisms. The RFC also notes that a site can simply announce its EID-Prefixes into the DFZ as routable EIDs, but this defeats LISP's goal of reducing global routing state, so it is not seen as a long-term solution.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of conversations. The tricky one is when someone with an old address writes to someone with a new address that old mailboxes cannot find.

sections.title: Proxy-ITRs and Proxy-ETRs
sections.content:
A Proxy-ITR advertises highly aggregated EID-Prefix space into the legacy Internet and encapsulates traffic it attracts toward the destination RLOCs. Proxy-ITRs should be deployed close to non-LISP sites rather than close to LISP sites, which limits the scope of the new routes and spreads the load. Traffic can be shared by announcing the same address from several Proxy-ITRs using IP Anycast.

The return path is asymmetric. The LISP site's ITR finds the original sender is not a LISP site and sends replies natively, so replies do not pass through the Proxy-ITR. That keeps the Proxy-ITR simple.

A Proxy-ETR is used the other way. An ITR is configured to encapsulate traffic for non-LISP destinations to a Proxy-ETR, which decapsulates and forwards it natively. Two reasons to do so are avoiding strict Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) failures and hopping over networks that lack the desired IP version. A Proxy-ETR should verify the inner source EID against configured LISP sites to prevent spoofed sources.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper stands near the old-style neighbors and wraps their letters in a special envelope. Another helper opens the special envelopes and drops the letters in the regular mail.

sections.title: LISP-NAT
sections.content:
LISP-NAT is a limited form of NAT. It lets a site with non-routable EIDs (LISP-NR) talk to non-LISP sites by replacing the source address with a globally routable one (a LISP-R EID), keeping a table so returning packets can be translated back. Sites using RFC 1918 private addresses can use it to talk to both LISP and non-LISP sites. It is not needed for LISP-R sources, whose addresses are already routable.

In the RFC's example, a site with the LISP-NR EID prefix 203.0.113.0/24 is also given 192.0.2.0/24. The address 192.0.2.1 is used as the site's RLOC and 192.0.2.2 to 192.0.2.254 form the translation pool. Host 203.0.113.2 is rewritten to 192.0.2.2.

A side effect is that a host may have two EIDs, so name-to-address directories may need changing. The RFC says using Proxy-ITRs can mitigate this, because the LISP-NR EID can then be reached in all cases.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a front desk that gives your outgoing mail a different return address, and remembers who it belongs to so replies reach you.

sections.title: Choosing a Mechanism and Security Notes
sections.content:
With LISP-NAT, the site manages its own interworking. With Proxy-ITRs, the site need not manage EID advertisement in the DFZ, at the cost of possible added stretch for non-LISP senders. Proxy-ETRs are optional and mainly assist LISP-NR sites already relying on Proxy-ITRs. Because Proxy-ITRs belong near non-LISP sites and Proxy-ETRs near LISP sites, they are best decoupled.

Proxy-ITRs and Proxy-ETRs will likely be run by other organizations, so the quality of service of the provider should be checked. Proxy-ITRs can inspect traffic and could help drop malicious traffic when an ETR requests it, which the RFC says needs more experimentation. LISP-NAT hides the real LISP-NR EID behind the pool addresses. For uRPF, a provider can use a looser check or a static route, or the site can send everything through a Proxy-ETR so the outer source is its RLOC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each helper has a job, and since other companies will usually run them, you should pick a good one and watch out for strict guards who check return addresses.
